solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Look closely at uranium splitting by itself

indicators.note: uranium's letter splits the phrase in two by going inside it

parts.note: per se = by itself, in itself
U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: A physicist watches an atom of uranium undergo fission all on its own.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is spontaneous nuclear fission; the splitting is done to the phrase, not the atom.
explanation.definitionFit: To peruse is to read or examine something closely.

clue.text: Show internet users normal stomach having just given birth

parts.note: to post something online is to show it to internet users
par = the normal standard, as in 'feeling below par'

explanation.surface: A new mother shares photos of her stomach online to show it is back to normal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a social-media post about a post-pregnancy body, which is exactly what the answer describes.
explanation.definitionFit: Postpartum means in the period just after childbirth.

clue.text: Fixing bush in hedge that's lost its crown

indicators.note: the crown is the top of a down entry, so the first letter goes

parts.note: privet is the classic hedging shrub

explanation.surface: A gardener repairs a hedge whose top has been cut off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixing' looks like a verb about repairing the hedge; it is a noun, a fastener.
explanation.definitionFit: A rivet is a metal pin used to fasten plates together: a fixing.

clue.text: Clearly utter gluttony for one painful condition

indicators.note: gluttony is one example of a sin

parts.note: gluttony is one of the seven deadly sins
gout is a painful inflammation of the joints

explanation.surface: A doctor warns plainly that overeating leads to a painful illness.
explanation.walkthrough: Gout was long blamed on rich food, so gluttony and gout sit naturally together in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal verb: to sing out is to shout or call so that everyone hears.

clue.text: Irritating underwear one has on right for gala

indicators.note: the A is placed on, i.e. attached ahead of, the rest
the right-hand end of 'gala', its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone complains about scratchy underwear they have to wear to a gala.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One has' reads as 'somebody owns', but it is I'VE, the speaker's 'I have'. 'Right for gala' is not a proper outfit but the rightmost letter of GALA.
explanation.definitionFit: Abrasive means harsh and grating, so irritating.

clue.text: Mark employed by memsahib in disguise?

indicators.note: the answer is held within, used by, the following words

explanation.surface: A European woman in colonial India disguises herself with a forehead mark.
explanation.walkthrough: A memsahib was a European married woman in colonial India; a bindi would be her disguise, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A bindi is a decorative mark worn on the forehead, especially by Hindu women.

clue.text: Hail sprayed CalMac crossing west of Islay

indicators.note: the letters of CALMAC are scattered
the scattered letters go across I, holding it
the westernmost, i.e. first, letter of Islay

explanation.surface: A CalMac ferry heading to Islay is drenched by hail and spray.
explanation.walkthrough: CalMac (Caledonian MacBrayne) runs the ferries to Scotland's west-coast islands, including Islay. 'Hail' is weather in the surface but a verb of praise in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonyms as verbs: to hail a hero is to greet them with loud public praise.

clue.text: Cushion you stand on the back of in church, showing disrespect

parts.note: an insole cushions the foot inside a shoe

indicators.note: a word's back is its rear end, so only its final letter is taken

explanation.surface: Someone stands on a kneeler cushion in church, a disrespectful act.
explanation.walkthrough: The church cushion suggests a hassock, but the one you stand on is an insole.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: cheek or rudeness towards someone who is owed respect.

clue.text: Most upset after low grade for this?

definitions.text: Most upset after low grade for this?

parts.note: E is a low mark on an A-to-E scale

indicators.note: 'after' means following in time, so in the entry the upset word follows the grade

explanation.surface: A student is most upset after a poor grade: in what?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: an exam is the thing you would be upset about after getting an E.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue asks what test leaves a student most upset after a bad mark, and the wordplay builds that very test.

clue.text: Stylish couch brought over mid-broadcast

parts.note: a couch is somewhere to lie, a bed
on air = in the middle of broadcasting

explanation.surface: A smart sofa is carried into a studio while the programme is live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought over' sounds like delivery; it reverses BED.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from Old French 'de bon air', of good bearing: smart and suave.

clue.text: Clue beginning with this spotted around competition?

parts.note: an event is a competition, as at a sports meeting

explanation.surface: A setter describes a clue that starts with a word spotted around some contest.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points to this very grid: 17 down is the clue that begins with the word 'This'.
explanation.definitionFit: 17 down opens with 'This', so the clue beginning with 'this' is seventeen.

clue.text: Rib much appreciated with green salad on the side

parts.note: cos is a variety of lettuce (romaine)

explanation.surface: A diner thanks the waiter for a rib dish served with a side salad.
explanation.walkthrough: The menu surface makes 'rib' a cut of meat; here it is the anatomical term. 'Ta' is British slang for thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist term: anatomists use the Latin word for a rib, as in 'intercostal' muscles between the ribs.

clue.text: Knock over house with good grounds as if compelled

parts.note: HO is the abbreviation for house
logically = with good reasoning behind it

explanation.surface: Someone justifies knocking a house down because they had good grounds for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knock over house' reads as demolition, but 'over' only reverses the knock.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something pathologically means doing it compulsively, as if one cannot help it.

clue.text: Small amount, small being significant

parts.note: S = small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A small thing can still count for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small' appears twice: the first is part of the definition, the second gives S.
explanation.definitionFit: A smattering is a small amount, of knowledge or of something scattered.

clue.text: Early aviator misplaces west at 90 degrees

definitions.note: RIGHT stands for 'right-angled' here, as in 'at right angles'.

indicators.note: the aviator loses the W for west

parts.note: the Wright brothers made the first powered flight in 1903

explanation.surface: A pioneer pilot loses his bearings, mistaking west for a right-angle turn.
explanation.walkthrough: A navigation surface: 'west' and '90 degrees' sound like compass bearings, but west is just the W to drop.
explanation.definitionFit: A right angle is 90 degrees, so something at right angles is at 90 degrees.

clue.text: Holding diamonds, try to make 7 hearts? Let's hope not

parts.note: to go for a bid of seven hearts, a grand slam in bridge
D = diamonds, as in card notation

explanation.surface: A bridge player holding diamonds dreads having to make a grand slam in hearts.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, seven hearts is a contract to win all thirteen tricks; going for it is a bid. The D slips in after GO.
explanation.definitionFit: God forbid! is an exclamation meaning 'let's hope that doesn't happen'.

clue.text: Notice explosive device in place mostly targeting character

indicators.note: HOME loses its last letter
the explosive goes inside the place

parts.note: HOME, a place, without its E

explanation.surface: A security alert: an explosive device has been noticed in a location, aimed at some figure.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a bomb threat aimed at a person; the answer is the Latin 'to the man', a debating term.
explanation.definitionFit: An ad hominem argument attacks the person's character rather than their case.

clue.text: This year's silly craze

indicators.note: the letters are made foolish, rearranged

explanation.surface: A commentator dismisses this year's fad as foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s is just 'is', joining the wordplay to the definition; 10 across points to this clue as the one that begins with 'This'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hysteria is a wild collective frenzy, a craze.

clue.text: Snare drum beaten ready for battle

indicators.note: the letters are knocked about, as a drum is beaten

explanation.surface: A military drummer beats out the call to arms.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator is perfectly in character: a snare drum is beaten, and so are its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Troops under arms are armed and ready to fight.

clue.text: Report of private antipathy

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so we want the sound

parts.note: a ranker is a soldier in the ranks, a private

explanation.surface: A soldier writes up his dislike of a fellow private.
explanation.walkthrough: RANKER and RANCOUR match in a non-rhotic British accent. 'Private' is not secret; it is the soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Rancour is bitter, long-held ill will: antipathy.

clue.text: Labour's position on Conservative split

parts.note: the Labour Party sits on the political left

explanation.surface: A political commentator describes Labour's stance on a divided Conservative party.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour is Britain's main left-of-centre party, the Conservatives its main right-wing one.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleft is a past participle of cleave: split.

clue.text: Shackles one must escape performing Piaf number?

indicators.note: the I for one gets out of the shackles

explanation.surface: Escape artist performs to a song by Édith Piaf.
explanation.walkthrough: Édith Piaf was the great French singer; a number of hers is a French song, hence the question mark for a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Chanson is French for song, the genre Piaf sang.

clue.text: Noble English king rather plump — illustration showing otherwise?

explanation.surface: A portrait flatters a stout English king, painting him as anything but plump.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry VIII hovers over the surface, but the king is only REX.
explanation.definitionFit: A counterexample is an instance that shows a general claim to be false.

clue.text: American casualty contracted fungal disease

parts.note: ER, the emergency room, is the American casualty department

explanation.surface: A US hospital patient has caught a fungal infection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Casualty' is the British name for a hospital's emergency department; Americans call it the ER. It is not an injured person.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergot is a fungal disease of rye and other cereals.

clue.text: Friendly correspondent eschews second page for discipline

indicators.note: the second of the two Ps is dropped

parts.note: a pen pal is a friend you write to
P = page, the second P removed

explanation.surface: A pen pal skips a page of their letter, earning a telling-off.
explanation.walkthrough: PENPAL has two Ps; 'second' tells you to drop the later one.
explanation.definitionFit: Penal means relating to punishment, so used for discipline.

clue.text: People considered one article

definitions.meaning: an informal phrase for a romantic couple, two people seen as a unit
a thing, one entry on a list

explanation.surface: A group of people is being treated as a single object.
explanation.walkthrough: A couple who are dating are said to be an item.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: an idiom for a pair seen as a couple, and a plain synonym for a single thing or entry.

clue.text: Advanced piece of footwear for cycling against the rules

indicators.note: the last letter is cycled round to the front

explanation.surface: A cyclist wears an unusual shoe that breaks the rules of the race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For cycling' sounds like cycling shoes; in fact ABOOT rotates, its T moving to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a taboo thing is forbidden by custom, which is breaking the unwritten rules.

clue.text: Sliding scales sliding as originally devised

indicators.note: the letters are rearranged, worked into something new

explanation.surface: A music teacher describes scales that slide, as first conceived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sliding' appears twice: the first is part of the definition, the second is fodder. Glissandi is the Italian plural of glissando.
explanation.definitionFit: A glissando is a rapid slide up or down a run of notes, a sliding scale.

clue.text: Youth on Vespa perhaps inspiring lady with steady speed

parts.note: mods were 1960s British youths who rode Vespa and Lambretta scooters
Erato, the Muse of lyric poetry

explanation.surface: A young man on a scooter, carrying a woman, rides at a sensible pace.
explanation.walkthrough: An 'inspiring lady' is a Muse; Erato is the one crosswords use most.
explanation.definitionFit: Moderato is the musical instruction to play at a moderate pace.

clue.text: Unwrapping sport shoes, free to run?

indicators.note: strips the wrapping, the outer letters, off FUNCLOGS

parts.note: sport = fun, as in 'said in sport'

explanation.surface: Someone takes off their sports shoes so they are free to go for a run.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about running shoes; the definition means clearing a blocked drain so water can run.
explanation.definitionFit: To unclog a pipe is to free it so liquid can run through.
